lead: Speed is everywhere on a plant floor: motor shafts, turbine rotors, paper rolls. Three cheap ways turn speed into an electrical reading. A tachogenerator is a small generator whose voltage rises with speed. A stroboscope flashes light at a known rate and freezes the shaft for the eye. Variable-frequency sensors carry the measurement in a signal's frequency, read by a counter or a frequency-to-voltage circuit.
prereq: Faraday's law of induction from basic physics, and the first- and second-order response from Unit 1, Foundations: Sensor Characteristics and Errors.

blocks.text: A tachogenerator is a small machine coupled to the shaft. A permanent magnet gives a constant field, so the induced emf depends only on speed.

blocks.where: E is the generated emf in volts (V); ω is the angular speed in rad/s; K is the machine constant in V·s/rad.

blocks.text: The DC output ripples at f<sub>ripple</sub> = S n / 60, with S commutator segments and n the speed in rpm. An RC filter with cutoff 1/(2πRC) well below f<sub>ripple</sub> smooths it.
Loading is the main error: the meter draws current I and the armature resistance R<sub>a</sub> drops V = E − I R<sub>a</sub>, so a low-impedance meter reads low. Use a high-impedance meter.

An AC tachogenerator has no commutator or brushes. Its amplitude rises with speed and its frequency is f = p n / 60, with p the number of pole pairs and n the speed in rpm. Rectify and filter it, or count the frequency.
A stroboscope is a xenon tube flashing at a rate f set by an oscillator. Paint z marks on the shaft; the eye sees a mark only when a flash lights it.

blocks.where: f is the flash rate in flashes per second (Hz); z is the number of marks painted on the shaft; n is the true speed in rpm; k = 1, 2, 3, … The image looks still whenever this holds.

blocks.text: At k = 1 the dial reads the true speed. At k = 2 or 3 the image is still but you see two or three copies of the mark, and the dial reads two or three times the true speed. At a whole-number fraction of the fundamental you see one still mark again and read half, or a third, of the true speed. This is aliasing.

Set the flash rate high, well above the expected speed, and lower it. The first single still image you reach is the true speed, f = z n / 60. A slow drift means the rate is slightly off, which lets you tune exactly.
Uses: calibrating tachometers, checking fan blades, watching a loudspeaker cone, inspecting printing registration.

A vibrating wire of length L, tension T and mass per length μ vibrates at f = (1/2L)√(T/μ), so pressure on a capsule becomes a frequency. A reluctance pick-up facing a toothed wheel gives one pulse per tooth.

Frequency signals travel well: cable resistance and amplifier gain do not change the count. A counter gates pulses for a time T<sub>g</sub> and shows N = f × T<sub>g</sub> counts, so the resolution is 1/N.

blocks.where: V<sub>out</sub> is the average DC output in volts; V<sub>ref</sub> is the pulse height in volts; T is the fixed pulse width in seconds set by a monostable; f<sub>in</sub> is the input frequency in Hz.

blocks.text: The formula holds for f<sub>in</sub> ≤ 1/T; above 1/T the pulses run together, the monostable stays high, and V<sub>out</sub> flattens at V<sub>ref</sub>. Set T for the highest frequency you expect to measure.
One monostable plus an RC averaging filter turns any frequency sensor into a DC voltage read as speed, force or pressure. Counting pulses in position encoders is the digital alternative.

figure.caption: The shaft drives a small generator; its AC is rectified and filtered to a DC voltage that the voltmeter reads as speed. Notice that the filter sits between the rectifier and the meter.

spec.aria: A shaft drives a tachogenerator whose AC voltage is rectified and filtered to a DC voltage read by a voltmeter as speed.

examples.question: A DC tachogenerator with K = 0.05 V/(rad/s) runs at 1500 rpm; the commutator has 12 segments. Find (a) the emf, (b) the ripple frequency, (c) where to put the filter cutoff.
steps: Cutoff near 30 Hz, a tenth of the ripple, damps it about ten times while the speed signal passes.
examples.answer: 7.85 V at 1500 rpm, ripple at 300 Hz, cutoff near 30 Hz.
examples.check:
import math
n = 1500.0
omega = n * 2 * math.pi / 60
K = 0.05
E = K * omega
segments = 12
f_ripple = segments * n / 60
print(round(omega, 2))
print(round(E, 2))
print(round(f_ripple, 2))

examples.question: A pick-up on a 60-tooth gear feeds 200 µs pulses of height 5 V to an RC averaging filter. The output is 0.25 V. Find the pulse frequency and the shaft speed in rpm.
steps: One pulse per tooth: n = 60 f<sub>in</sub> / 60 = 250 rpm.
examples.answer: The pulse frequency is 250 Hz and the shaft turns at 250 rpm.
examples.check:
Vout = 0.25
Vref = 5.0
T = 200e-6
fin = Vout / (Vref * T)
teeth = 60
n = fin * 60 / teeth
print(round(fin, 2))
print(round(n, 2))

traps: rad/s against rpm: dropping the 2π/60 factor makes the answer wrong by 9.55 times. Convert first, always.
The stroboscope also freezes the image at k = 2 or 3, so the dial shows two or three times the true speed. Lower the rate from a high value and stop at the first single still image.
A low-impedance voltmeter loads a DC tachogenerator and reads low because of the I R<sub>a</sub> drop; examiners ask why the open-circuit emf is quoted.
In a frequency-to-voltage converter the scale is V<sub>ref</sub> × T, not V<sub>ref</sub> × T<sub>g</sub>; mixing the pulse width with the counter gate time gives a wrong volts-per-hertz figure.

quiz.q: What is the output of a DC tachogenerator proportional to?
quiz.a: The emf E = K ω, proportional to angular speed; K is the machine constant in V·s/rad.

quiz.q: Why does an AC tachogenerator need a rectifier before a moving-coil voltmeter?
quiz.a: A moving-coil meter responds to average current. An AC signal averages to zero, so rectify and filter it into DC first.

quiz.q: A tachogenerator has K = 0.08 V/(rad/s) and turns at 900 rpm. Find its emf.
A 250 Hz pulse train of 200 µs width and 5 V height feeds a frequency-to-voltage converter. Find the average output.
A stroboscope shows a still image of the painted mark at 1200 flashes/min and again at 2400 flashes/min. What can you conclude about the speed?
quiz.a: The pair fits 1200 rpm with k = 1 and 2, but also 600 rpm with k = 2 and 4, so it is ambiguous. Lower the rate from a high value and stop at the first single still image, then confirm with a second method.

quiz.q: A counter gates a 250 Hz signal for 1 s. What is the count and the resolution?
quiz.a: N = f T<sub>g</sub> = 250 counts, with ±1 count uncertainty, so the resolution is 1/250 = 0.4 %.

beyond: Not for the exam. Variable-reluctance and Hall wheel-speed sensors in cars, vibrating-wire pressure cells on dams, and stroboscopic inspection on printing presses use these ideas. Encoders and resolver-to-digital chips have replaced most tachogenerators in new drives.
